entries.f64143c8e314a012bf4daea0ff4680002ea08dbf: <div sID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="124" osisID="Ps.124" sID="Ps.124"/> <div eID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12967" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12968" type="x-p"/> David penned this psalm (we suppose) upon occasion of some great deliverance which God wrought for him and his people from some very threatening danger, which was likely to have involved them all in ruin, whether by foreign invasion, or intestine insurrection, is not certain; whatever it was he seems to have been himself much affected, and very desirous to affect others, with the goodness of God, in making a way for them to escape. To him he is careful to give all the glory, and takes none to himself as conquerors usually do. I. He here magnifies the greatness of the danger they were in, and of the ruin they were at the brink of, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He gives God the glory of their escape, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6-Ps.124.7">ver. 6, 7 compared with ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.2">2</reference>. III. He takes encouragement thence to trust in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">ver. 8</reference>. In singing this psalm, besides the application of it to any particular deliverance wrought for us and our people, in our days and the days of our fathers, we may have in our thoughts the great work of our redemption by Jesus Christ, by which we were rescued from the powers of darkness.
entries.321983f2c54d6227d2fb17a45c70f241773504c5: <div eID="gen12968" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12967" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of God's People.</title> <div sID="gen12969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> If <hi type="italic">it had not been</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> who was on our side, now may Israel say; 2 If <hi type="italic">it had not been</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> who was on our side, when men rose up against us: <hi type="super">3</hi> Then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us: <hi type="super">4</hi> Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul: <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the proud waters had gone over our soul. <div eID="gen12969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12970" type="x-p"/> The people of God, being here called upon to praise God for their deliverance, are to take notice, <div eID="gen12970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12971" type="x-p"/> I. Of the malice of men, by which they were reduced to the very brink of ruin. Let Israel say that there was but a step between them and death: the more desperate the disease appears to have been the more does the skill of the Physician appear in the cure. Observe, 1. Whence the threatening danger came: <hi type="italic">Men rose up against us,</hi> creatures of our own kind, and yet bent upon our ruin. <hi type="italic">Homo homini lupus—Man is a wolf to man.</hi> No marvel that the red dragon, the roaring lion, should seek to swallow us up; but that men should thirst after the blood of men, Absalom after the blood of his own father, that a woman should be drunk with the blood of saints, is what, with St. John, we may wonder at with great admiration. From men we may expect humanity, yet there are those whose <hi type="italic">tender mercies are cruel.</hi> But what was the matter with these men? Why <hi type="italic">their wrath was kindled against us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.3">v. 3</reference>); something or other they were angry at, and then no less would serve than the destruction of those they had conceived a displeasure against. <hi type="italic">Wrath is cruel and anger is outrageous.</hi> Their wrath was kindled as fire ready to consume us. They were proud; and <hi type="italic">the wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor.</hi> They were daring in their attempt; they <hi type="italic">rose up against us,</hi> rose in rebellion, with a resolution to <hi type="italic">swallow us up</hi> alive. 2. How far it went, and how fatal it would have been if it had gone a little further: "We should have been devoured as a lamb by a lion, not only slain, but <hi type="italic">swallowed up,</hi> so that there would have been no relics of us remaining, swallowed up with so much haste, ere we were aware, that we should have gone down alive to the pit. We should have been deluged as the low grounds by a land-flood or the sands by a high spring-tide." This similitude he dwells upon, with the ascents which bespeak this a song of degrees, or risings, like the rest. <hi type="italic">The waters had overwhelmed us.</hi> What of us? Why <hi type="italic">the stream had gone over our souls,</hi> our lives, our comforts, all that is dear to us. What waters? Why <hi type="italic">the proud waters.</hi> God suffers the enemies of his people sometimes to prevail very far against them, that his own power may appear the more illustrious in their deliverance. <div eID="gen12971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12972" type="x-p"/> II. Of the goodness of God, by which they were rescued from the very brink of ruin: "<hi type="italic">The Lord was on our side;</hi> and, <hi type="italic">if he had not been so,</hi> we should have been undone." 1. "God was on our side; he took our part, espoused our cause, and appeared for us. He was our helper, and a very present help, a help on our side, nigh at hand. He was with us, not only for us, but among us, and commander-in-chief of our forces." 2. That God was Jehovah; there the emphasis lies. "If it had not been Jehovah himself, a God of infinite power and perfection, that had undertaken our deliverance, our enemies would have overpowered us." Happy the people, therefore, whose God is Jehovah, a God all-sufficient. Let Israel say this, to his honour, and resolve never to forsake him.
entries.bc496f622c712b392b1aaf2d77e3439feef89a21: <div eID="gen12972" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of God's People.</title> <div sID="gen12973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who hath not given us <hi type="italic">as</hi> a prey to their teeth. <hi type="super">7</hi> Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped. 8 Our help <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who made heaven and earth. <div eID="gen12973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12974" type="x-p"/> Here the psalmist further magnifies the great deliverance God had lately wrought for them. <div eID="gen12974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12975" type="x-p"/> I. That their hearts might be the more enlarged in thankfulness to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord.</hi> God is the author of all our deliverances, and therefore he must have the glory of them. We rob him of his due if we do not return thanks to him. And we are the more obliged to praise him because we had such a narrow escape. We were delivered, 1. Like a lamb out of the very jaws of a beast of prey: God <hi type="italic">has not given us as a prey to their teeth,</hi> intimating that they had no power over God's people but what was given them from above. They could not be a prey to their teeth unless God gave them up, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they were rescued, because God would not suffer them to be ruined. 2. Like <hi type="italic">a bird,</hi> a little bird (the word signifies a sparrow), <hi type="italic">out of the snare of the fowler.</hi> The enemies are very subtle and spiteful; they lay snares for God's people, to bring them into sin and trouble, and to hold them there. Sometimes they seem to have prevailed so far as to gain their point. God's people are taken in the snare, and are as unable to help themselves out as any weak and silly bird is; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> is God's time to appear for their relief, when all other friends fail; then God breaks the snare, and turns the counsel of the enemies into foolishness: <hi type="italic">The snare is broken and so we are delivered.</hi> Isaac was saved when he lay ready to be sacrificed. <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh—in the mount of the Lord it shall be seen.</hi> <div eID="gen12975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12976" type="x-p"/> II. That their hearts, and the hearts of others, might be the more encouraged to trust in God in the like dangers (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our help is in the name of the Lord.</hi> David had directed us (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">Ps. cxxi. 2</reference>) to depend upon God for help as to our personal concerns—<hi type="italic">My help is in the name of the Lord;</hi> here as to the concerns of the public—Our <hi type="italic">help is so.</hi> It is a comfort to all that lay the interests of God's Israel near their hearts that Israel's God is the same that made the world, and therefore will have a church in the world, and can secure that church in times of the greatest danger and distress. In him therefore let the church's friends put their confidence, and they shall not be put to confusion.  <chapter eID="Ps.124"/> <div eID="gen12976" type="x-p"/>

entries.6f656fee4cc97d5c4ea4e2b36560642a9e84f357: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7003"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 124</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8">Psa 124:1-8</reference>. The writer, for the Church, praises God for past, and expresses trust for future, deliverance from foes.</title> <div sID="gen10746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7003"/><hi type="bold">1-2. on our side--</hi>for us (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.9">Psa 56:9</reference>).<div eID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>or, "oh! let Israel" <div eID="gen10747" type="x-p"/>
entries.8116bd8e1bffade7750d32cf0a3724debd645cf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7005"/><div sID="gen10749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7005"/><hi type="bold">3. Then--</hi>that is, the time of our danger.<div eID="gen10749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quick--</hi>literally, "living" (<reference osisRef="Num.16.32">Nu 16:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.33">33</reference>), description of ferocity. <div eID="gen10750" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6fee63d65c21d178e92eeb39e761bbecfa8ad7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7006"/><div sID="gen10751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7006"/>4-5. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen10751" type="x-p"/>
entries.9262929306fcd49a0903d5f22ebe3c2e4948d6f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7008"/><div sID="gen10753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7008"/>6-7. The figure is changed to that of a rapacious wild beast (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>), and then of a fowler (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.3">Psa 91:3</reference>), and complete escape is denoted by breaking the net. <div eID="gen10753" type="x-p"/>
entries.64d1b241c096f0907165d2bdc0fd42915bb08c90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7009"/><div sID="gen10754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7009"/>8. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name--</hi>in the usual sense (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">20:1</reference>). He thus places over against the great danger the omnipotent God, and drowns, as it were in an anthem, the wickedness of the whole world and of hell, just as a great fire consumes a little drop of water [Luther]. <chapter eID="Ps.124"/>

entries.cb4104bbad4e54d7c8b1acd2d3dfbd246f9aab6f: <div eID="gen23054" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23055" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23056" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23056" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23055" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23057" type="x-p"/> A thanksgiving of the godly for extraordinary deliverances, <reference osisRef="Psa.124.1-Psa.124.4">Psa 124:1-4</reference>. The great danger they were in, <reference osisRef="Psa.124.7">Psa 124:7</reference>. Their confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.124.8">Psa 124:8</reference>. <div eID="gen23057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23058" type="x-p"/> In our present Hebrew copies this Psalm is attributed to David, לדוד ledavid; but this inscription is wanting in three of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., as also in the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, Ethiopic, and Arabic; and in most of the ancient fathers, Greek and Latin, who found no other inscription in their copies of the text than A Psalm of degrees. It was composed long after David's days; and appears to be either a thanksgiving for their deliverance from the Babylonish captivity, or for a remarkable deliverance from some potent and insidious enemy after their return to Judea. Or, what appears to be more likely, it is a thanksgiving of the Jews for their escape from the general massacre intended by Haman, prime minister of Ahasuerus, king of Persia. See the whole Book of Esther. <div eID="gen23058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23059" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23060" type="x-p"/> If it had not been the Lord - If God had not, in a very especial manner, supported and defended us, we had all been swallowed up alive, and destroyed by a sudden destruction, so that not one would have been left. This might refer to the plot against the whole nation of the Jews by Haman, in the days of Mordecai and Esther; when by his treacherous schemes the Jews, wheresoever dispersed in the provinces of Babylon, were all to have been put to death in one day. This may here be represented under the figure of an earthquake, when a chasm is formed, and a whole city and its inhabitants are in a moment swallowed up alive.
entries.235d5a920e5d52b9f113ab73140dfc82e9279243: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23061" type="x-p"/> Then the proud waters - The proud Haman had nearly brought the flood of desolation over our lives.
entries.dab6681b52b421291b2545d07d54852900e924ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23062" type="x-p"/> Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare - This is a fine image; and at once shows the weakness of the Jews, and the cunning of their adversaries. Haman had laid the snare completely for them; humanly speaking there was no prospect of their escape: but the Lord was on their side; and the providence that induced Ahasuerus to call for the book of the records of the kingdom to be read to him, as well indeed as the once very improbable advancement of Esther to the throne of Persia, was the means used by the Lord for the preservation of the whole Jewish people from extermination. God thus broke the snare, and the bird escaped; while the poacher was caught in his own trap, and executed. See the Book of Esther, which is probably the best comment on this Psalm.
entries.92fce3a5b698953007dd40167544eab981c1dcb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23063" type="x-p"/> Our help is in the name of the Lord - בשום מימרא דיי beshum meywra depai, Chaldee, "In the name of the Word of the Lord." So in the second verse, "Unless the Word of the Lord had been our Helper:" the substantial Word; not a word spoken, or a prophecy delivered, but the person who was afterwards termed Ὁ Λογος του Θεου, the Word of God. This deliverance of the Jews appears to me the most natural interpretation of this Psalm: and probably Mordecai was the author.  <chapter eID="Ps.124"/> <div eID="gen23063" type="x-p"/>

entries.0bda2b13b1ea08ab4dc7f2ade3de67fa423e54c8: <div eID="gen10184" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Deliverer from Death in Waters and in a Snare</title> <div sID="gen10185" type="x-p"/> The statement “the stream had gone over our soul” of this fifth Son of degrees, coincides with the statement “our soul is full enough” of the fourth; the two Psalms also meet in the synonymous new formations גּאיונים and זידונים, which also look very much as though they were formed in allusion to contemporary history. The לדוד is wanting in the lxx, <hi type="italic">Codd. Alex.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Vat.</hi>, here as in <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9">Psa 122:1-9</reference>, and with the exception of the Targum is wanting in general in the ancient versions, and therefore is not so much as established as a point of textual criticism. It is a Psalm in the manner of the Davidic Psalms, to which it is closely allied in the metaphors of the overwhelming waters, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.17">Psa 18:17</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">Psa 144:7</reference>), Psa 69:2., and of the little bird; cf. also on לוּלי <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, on אדם used of hostile men <reference osisRef="Ps.56.12">Psa 56:12</reference>, on בּלע חיּים <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, on בּרוּך ה <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference>; Psa 31:22. This beautiful song makes its modern origin known by its Aramaizing character, and by the delight, after the manner of the later poetry, in all kinds of embellishments of language. The art of the form consists less in strophic symmetry than in this, that in order to take one step forward it always goes back half a step. Luther’s imitation (1524), “Were God not with us at this time” (<hi type="italic">Wäre Gott nicht mit uns diese Zeit</hi>), bears the inscription “The true believers’ safeguard.”
entries.7cd20466fd378e895739f4a2e102edc8b3c4701f: <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.5">Psa 124:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10186" type="x-p"/> It is commonly rendered, “If it had not been Jahve who was for us.” But, notwithstanding the subject that is placed first (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.23.13">Gen 23:13</reference>), the שׁ belongs to the לוּלי; since in the Aramaizing Hebrew (cf. on the other hand <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen 31:42</reference>) לוּלי שׁ (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">lawlâ an</hi>) signifies <hi type="italic">nisi</hi> (prop. <hi type="italic">nisi quod</hi>), as in the Aramaic (דּ) שׁ (לואי) לוי, <hi type="italic">o si</hi> (prop. <hi type="italic">o si quod</hi>). The אזי, peculiar to this Psalm in the Old Testament, instead of אז follows the model of the dialectic אדין, Arab. <hi type="italic">iḏan</hi>, Syr. <hi type="italic">hāden</hi> (הידין, הדין). In order to begin the apodosis of לוּלי (לוּלא) emphatically the older language makes use of the confirmatory כּי, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen 31:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.10">Gen 43:10</reference>; here we have אזי (well rendered by the lxx ἄρα), as in Psa 119:92. The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of היה לנו is <hi type="italic">raphe</hi> in both instances, according to the rule discussed above, p. 373. When men (אדם) rose up against Israel and their anger was kindled against them, they who were feeble in themselves over against the hostile world would have been swallowed up alive if they had not had Jahve for them, if they had not had Him on their side. This “swallowing up alive” is said elsewhere of Hades, which suddenly and forcibly snatches away its victims, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.12">Pro 1:12</reference>; here, however, as <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6">Psa 124:6</reference> shows, it is said of the enemies, who are represented as wild beasts. In <reference osisRef="Ps.124.4">Psa 124:4</reference> the hostile power which rolls over them is likened to an overflowing stream, as in Isa 8:7., the Assyrian. נחלה, a stream or river, is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>; it is first of all accusative: towards the stream (Num 34:5); then, however, it is also used as a nominative, like לילה, המּותה, and the like (cf. common Greek ἡ νύχθα, ἡ νεόντητα); so that  תה- is related to  ת- ( ה-) as  נה-,  מו- to  ן- and  ם- (Böttcher, §615). These latest Psalms are fond of such embellishments by means of adorned forms and Aramaic or Aramaizing words. זידונים is a word which is indeed not unhebraic in its formation, but is more indigenous to Chaldee; it is the Targum word for זדים in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">Psa 86:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.51">Psa 119:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.78">Psa 119:78</reference> (also in <reference osisRef="Ps.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference> for זרים), although according to Levy the MSS do not present זידונין but זידנין. In the passage before us the Targum renders: the king who is like to the proud waters (למוי זידוניּא) of the sea (Antiochus Epiphanes? - a Scholium explains οἱ ὑπερήφανοι). With reference to עבר before a plural subject, vid., Ges. §147.
entries.11344c661aae48ee3ec7eb00d4e8e2cc7a979214: <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6-Ps.124.8">Psa 124:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen10186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10187" type="x-p"/> After the fact of the divine succour has been expressed, in <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6">Psa 124:6</reference> follows the thanksgiving for it, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.124.7">Psa 124:7</reference> the joyful shout of the rescued one. In <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6">Psa 124:6</reference> the enemies are conceived of as beasts of prey on account of their bloodthirstiness, just as the worldly empires are in the Book of Daniel; in <reference osisRef="Ps.124.7">Psa 124:7</reference> as “fowlers” on account of their cunning. According to the punctuation it is not to be rendered: Our soul is like a bird that is escaped, in which case it would have been accented בפשׁנו כצפור, but: our soul (subject with <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi>) is as a bird (כּצפור as in Hos 11:11; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.32">Pro 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>, instead of the syntactically more usual כּצּפור) escaped out of the snare of him who lays snares (יוקשׁ, elsewhere יקושׁ, יקוּשׁ, a fowler, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.3">Psa 91:3</reference>). נשׁבר (with <hi type="italic">ā</hi> beside <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>) is <hi type="italic">3rd praet.</hi>: the snare was burst, and we - we became free. In <reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">Psa 124:8</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference>) the universal, and here pertinent thought, viz., the help of Israel is in the name of Jahve, the Creator of the world, i.e., in Him who is manifest as such and is continually verifying Himself, forms the epiphonematic close. Whether the power of the world seeks to make the church of Jahve like to itself or to annihilate it, it is not a disavowal of its God, but a faithful confession, stedfast even to death, that leads to its deliverance.  <chapter eID="Ps.124"/> <div eID="gen10187" type="x-p"/>

entries.03ab126d97a1b37133930b690b009b3366feef2c:
PSALM 124
The Church having been providentially delivered from extreme peril, David exhorts true believers to thanksgiving, and teaches them by this memorable example, that their safety depends solely upon the grace and power of God.
A Song of Degrees of David.
Psalm 124:1-5
1. But for Jehovah, who was on our side, may Israel now say; 2. But for Jehovah who was on our side, when men rose up against us; 3. They had then swallowed us up alive, when their wrath was kindled against us; 4. The waters had then overwhelmed us, the torrent had gone over our soul: 5. The proud waters
“Alors les eaux enfiees et impetueuses fussent,” etc. — Fr. “The swollen and impetuous waters had then,” etc. The epithet proud is applied to the waves of the sea in Job 38:11.
had then gone over our soul.
 
1. But for Jehovah, who was on our side. Some expositors think that this Psalm describes the very sad and calamitous condition of the Church when the, residue of the people were carried away into Babylon. This opinion is, however, without any good foundation for the complaints made, apply with equal propriety to the persecutions which the Church suffered under the tyranny of Antiochus Epiphanes. It is another objection to this interpretation, that the Psalm bears in its inscription the name of David, and historically recounts the deliverance which the people had obtained from extreme danger by the power of God. To get quit of this difficulty they observe, that what had not yet come to pass is described prophetically; but this is a forced conjecture, for the Prophets usually speak of things to come in a different manner. It is more probable that David here sets forth a known history, and exhorts the faithful to reflect upon the divine succor which they had already actually experienced. I dare not, however, limit what is here spoken to David’s time. It is indeed true that the heathen nations often waged war against the people of God, armed with such power as to come rushing upon them with the impetuosity of a deluge; but as David does not specify any particular instance, he is not, I conceive, to be understood as celebrating only some one deliverance, but in general all the instances in which God had succoured his Church. The heathen at many different times, as is well known, rose up against the Church, with such mighty hosts, that she was brought almost to the verge of destruction. David then represents as in a mirror the uncertain and changeable condition of the Church, just such as it had been from the beginning, to teach the faithful that its stability had not been owing to its own intrinsic strength, but that it had been preserved by the wonderful grace of God; and to habituate them to call upon God in the midst of dangers.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="124" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm was composed by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in the name and for the use of all the Church and people of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> as a thanksgiving for their deliverance from some eminent danger or dangers from proud and potent enemies. Many such they had in <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> time: but which of them is here intended, is hard to determine, and not worth the inquiry.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 IF <ns0:hi>it had not been</ns0:hi> the LORD who was on our side, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 129. 1.</ns0:note> now may Israel say:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then they had swallowed us up quick <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">They had speedily and utterly destroyed us, as <ns0:hi>Korah,</ns0:hi> &c. were <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 16.</ns0:note>, when their wrath was kindled against us.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then the proud waters <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Our enemies compared to <ns0:hi>proud waters,</ns0:hi> for their great multitude and swelling rage and mighty force.</ns0:note> had gone over our soul.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the LORD, who hath not given us <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> a prey to their teeth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">A Metaphor from wild beasts which tear and devour their prey with their teeth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Our soul is escaped <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 6. 5.</ns0:note> as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are escaped.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 121. 2.</ns0:note> Our help <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>

Poole.heading: PSAL. CXXIV. A song of degrees of David.
